June 9, 2026 
 
 
The Honorable Mehmet Oz 
Administrator 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services 
Hubert H. Humphrey Building 
200 Independence Avenue SW 
Washington, DC 20201 
 
 
Re:   
Comments of the Connected Health Initiative, Medicare and Medicaid Programs; 
Patient Protection and A2ordable Care Act; Interoperability Standards and Prior 
Authorization for Drugs (CMS-0062-P; RIN 0938-AV44; 91 Fed. Reg. 19890, April 14, 2026) 
 
Dear Administrator Oz: 
 
The Connected Health Initiative (CHI) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed 
rule issued by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) and the Assistant Secretary for 
Technology Policy and OPice of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology 
(ASTP/ONC) on interoperability standards and prior authorization for drugs.1 
 
CHI is a broad multistakeholder ePort that brings together patients, providers, payers, and 
technology innovators, including many small and medium-sized software developers, to advance a 
connected and interoperable health care system. Our comments focus on the proposed changes to 
the Medicare Promoting Interoperability (PI) Program, which fall within CHI's core interests in 
interoperability, patient access to health data, and the responsible use of digital health tools. 
 
I. 
Introduction and Statement of Interest 
 
CHI is a leading multistakeholder ePort dedicated to realizing the full potential of connected health 
technologies to improve patient outcomes, lower the cost of care, and expand access. CHIâ€™s 
participants include patients, providers, payers, and the technology developers who build the 
digital health tools that patients and clinicians rely on every day. Standardized, predictable, and 
openly accessible health data infrastructure beneï¬ts every participant in this ecosystem. 
CHI prioritizes interoperability and patient access to health data, the reduction of the burden that 
prior authorization imposes on patients, clinicians, and developers, and the responsible 
development and deployment of digital health and artiï¬cial intelligence (AI) tools. CHI has 
consistently urged the responsible expansion of application programming interface (API) based 
interoperability and the reduction of administrative burden across the health care system.  
 
1 Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and A2ordable Care Act; Interoperability Standards and Prior 
Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, 
Childrenâ€™s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualiï¬ed Health 
Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges, 91 Fed. Reg. 19890 (Apr. 14, 2026) (the â€œProposed Ruleâ€). 
2 
 
 
II. 
General Views of CHI 
 
CHIâ€™s overarching priority, in this rulemaking and across CMSâ€™ broader regulatory agenda, is the 
development of a connected care continuum in which patient data, clinical workï¬‚ows, and payer 
processes interoperate seamlessly across care settings and over the full course of a patientâ€™s care. 
When information follows the patient rather than remaining siloed in disconnected systems, 
clinicians can better coordinate care, patients can engage meaningfully in their own health, 
administrative friction such as prior authorization is reduced, and digital health tools, including 
remote patient monitoring, telehealth, and AI-enabled services, can deliver their full value. These 
priorities recur across CMS rulemakings, from interoperability and prior authorization, and the 
beneï¬t of any individual rule is magniï¬ed when its requirements remain consistent with those of 
the others. 
 
Accordingly, CHI supports a technology-neutral and standards-based approach to interoperability, 
robust patient and provider access to health data through Fast Healthcare Interoperability 
Resources (FHIR)-based APIs, the reduction of unnecessary administrative burden including prior 
authorization burden, symmetry and accountability between payer and provider technology, and 
alignment of requirements across programs so that technology can be built once and used 
everywhere. CHI assesses the proposals and requests for information in this proposed rule against 
these priorities. CHI also recognizes that realizing these priorities depends on realistic 
implementation timelines, careful attention to the cost and technical complexity that new 
requirements can impose on payers and providers alike, and a collaborative relationship between 
CMS and the regulated community. 
 
III. 
Speciï¬c Input of CHI on Various Proposals 
 
a. CHI supports extending electronic prior authorization to drugs and 
standardizing it on FHIR and the NCPDP standards 
 
Prior authorization remains one of the most signiï¬cant sources of delay to timely care and of 
administrative cost in the system. CHI supports CMSâ€™ proposal to require impacted payers to 
support electronic prior authorization for all drugs, to incorporate drugs covered under a medical 
beneï¬t into the Prior Authorization API, and to support the National Council for Prescription Drug 
Programs (NCPDP) SCRIPT, Formulary & Beneï¬t, and Real-Time Prescription Beneï¬t standards for 
drugs covered under a pharmacy beneï¬t.2 Standardized, API-based prior authorization built on 
FHIR reduces the manual work that consumes clinician time and delays patient access to 
medications. 
 
CHI encourages CMS to keep its requirements consistent across CMS programs and aligned with 
ASTP/ONC certiï¬cation criteria so that developers can build once and deploy across settings, 
rather than maintaining duplicative implementations for diPerent payers and programs. 
 
 
2 See 91 Fed. Reg. at 19892 (proposing to require impacted payers to support electronic prior authorization for all drugs, 
to incorporate drugs covered under a medical beneï¬t into the Prior Authorization API, and to support the NCPDP 
standards for drugs covered under a pharmacy beneï¬t). 
3 
 
b. CHI supports requiring the FHIR implementation guides and adopting FHIR for 
prior authorization transactions 
 
CHI supports CMSâ€™ proposal to require (rather than recommend) the Health Level Seven (HL7) FHIR 
Da Vinci implementation guides that underpin the interoperability APIs, and to permit impacted 
payers to use any unexpired adopted version of a required standard.3 Moving these implementation 
guides from recommended to required reduces variability and gives developers the predictability 
they need to build conformant products. CHI likewise supports CMSâ€™ proposal under the Health 
Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) Administrative Simpliï¬cation authority to 
adopt the FHIR standard and associated guides for the referral certiï¬cation and authorization and 
eligibility transactions associated with prior authorization for dental, professional, and institutional 
transactions.4 
 
CHI urges CMS and ASTP/ONC to coordinate version adoption and expiration timelines carefully so 
that the transition periods are workable. Where more than one unexpired version of a standard is 
adopted, developers and payers beneï¬t from a clearly communicated schedule and adequate 
overlap before older versions expire. 
 
c. CHI supports the centralized directory of payer API endpoints 
 
CHI has consistently emphasized that the full value of the interoperability APIs cannot be realized if 
developers, providers, and payers must locate one anotherâ€™s endpoints individually. CHI therefore 
supports CMSâ€™ proposal to require impacted payers to report their Patient Access, Provider 
Directory, Provider Access, Payer-to-Payer, and Prior Authorization API endpoints and related 
information to CMS for publication.5 A reliable, centralized, machine-readable endpoint directory is 
foundational to the Payer-to-Payer use case and materially lowers the discovery burden across the 
ecosystem. CHI encourages CMS to publish the directory in an openly accessible, standardized, 
and regularly updated form, and to keep the reporting requirements themselves lightweight. 
 
d. Payer-side and provider-side technology should be subject to comparable and 
consistent standards 
 
CHI reiterates that certiï¬ed technology used by providers and the corresponding technical 
interfaces on the payer side should be held to comparable standards so that electronic data 
exchange functions ePectively, particularly for electronic prior authorization. Interoperability works 
best when payer-side and provider-side technology advance together, rather than holding one side 
to obligations the other does not share. CHI therefore encourages CMS to pair API expectations 
with appropriate conformance testing and to work collaboratively with payers and developers to 
deï¬ne reasonable, achievable performance expectations that support near-real-time exchange. 
CHI recognizes that meeting such expectations involves real implementation cost and technical 
 
3 See 91 Fed. Reg. at 19893 (proposing to require implementation guides previously recommended and to permit use of 
any unexpired adopted version of a required standard). 
4 See 91 Fed. Reg. at 19896 (proposing under HIPAA Administrative Simpliï¬cation to adopt the FHIR standard and 
associated guides for the referral certiï¬cation and authorization and eligibility for a health plan transactions associated 
with prior authorization). 
5 See 91 Fed. Reg. at 19896 (proposing to require impacted payers to report Patient Access, Provider Directory, Provider 
Access, Payer-to-Payer, and Prior Authorization API endpoints and related information to CMS). 
4 
 
complexity for payers, and encourages CMS to develop any performance benchmarks 
collaboratively and to phase them in over an adequate timeline.  
 
e. CHI supports including small group market QHP issuers on the FF-SHOPs and 
aligning compliance across payers 
 
CHI supports CMSâ€™ goal of extending comparable interoperability and prior authorization 
protections to small group market Qualiï¬ed Health Plan (QHP) issuers on the Federally-facilitated 
Small Business Health Options Program (FF-SHOP) Exchanges.6  Patients should not be 
disadvantaged in their data access or prior authorization protections simply because of the market 
in which their coverage is oPered. At the same time, CHI recognizes that some aPected issuers may 
face meaningful implementation cost and operational complexity, and encourages CMS to extend 
these protections through a phased and adequately resourced timeline. CHI encourages CMS to 
retain a narrowly tailored exception mechanism, and to consider additional ï¬‚exibility, for any issuer, 
including genuine new entrants, that has not previously implemented the APIs. 
 
f. RFI on Electronic Event Notiï¬cations for Value-Based Care and Care 
Coordination 
 
CHI supports expanded use of electronic event notiï¬cations (commonly admission, discharge, and 
transfer, or ADT) as a tool for care coordination and value-based care. Timely notiï¬cation of care 
transitions is one of the highest-value, lowest-cost interventions available for reducing avoidable 
readmissions and closing gaps in care. 
 
CHI recommends that CMS and ASTP/ONC advance event notiï¬cations on a standardized, FHIR-
based foundation, which will allow notiï¬cations to be generated, routed, and consumed 
consistently across the ecosystem. Further, because patient-generated health data and the digital 
tools that capture it are central to modern care coordination, CHI encourages CMS to consider 
whether, with appropriate patient authorization and privacy safeguards, the universe of entities able 
to receive notiï¬cations could extend beyond traditional treating providers to include the care 
management platforms, remote monitoring services, and patient-authorized applications that 
increasingly support care transitions, while remaining attentive to the operational burden that 
broader distribution may place on the organizations that generate and send notiï¬cations. 
 
To the extent CMS considers health IT certiï¬cation criteria for notiï¬cation capabilities, CHI urges 
that any such criteria be FHIR-forward, align with the standards adopted elsewhere in this 
rulemaking so that developers can build once, and be supported by accessible testing tools. CHI 
supports encouraging more consistent delivery of notiï¬cations, and recommends that CMS favor 
collaborative and voluntary approaches over new enforcement obligations, calibrated so as not to 
impose disproportionate burden on developers, payers, and under-resourced facilities. 
 
g. RFI on Increasing Health Care Resiliency 
 
CHI shares CMSâ€™ concern about the escalating threat that hacking, ransomware, and other 
cyberattacks pose to the health care system and to electronic protected health information. CHI 
 
6 See 91 Fed. Reg. at 19895 (proposing to include small group market QHP issuers on the FF-SHOPs as impacted payers 
and to apply the existing API and prior authorization requirements to them). 
5 
 
supports strengthening the resiliency of the health care system through collaborative, largely 
voluntary measures developed together with payers, providers, and developers, and oPers the 
following recommendations: 
â€¢ 
First, CMS should anchor any resiliency expectations to existing, widely recognized 
frameworks rather than creating new and potentially conï¬‚icting requirements. The 
Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Healthcare and Public Health Sector 
Cybersecurity Performance Goals, the National Institute of Standards and Technology 
(NIST) Cybersecurity Framework, the Health Industry Cybersecurity Practices developed 
under Section 405(d), and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) 
Known Exploited Vulnerabilities guidance provide a coherent baseline. Aligning to these 
frameworks reduces compliance cost and improves security outcomes, particularly for the 
under-resourced and rural facilities that cannot absorb duplicative requirements. 
â€¢ 
Second, CHI reiterates its recommendation that HHS expand cybersecurity safe harbor 
protections to facilitate the donation of security tools, threat monitoring, and security 
training to under-resourced provider organizations, including in connection with remote 
monitoring and connected health deployments. As connected devices proliferate, 
cybersecurity is increasingly inseparable from digital health deployment, and outdated 
fraud and abuse rules should not stand in the way of arrangements designed to protect 
patient data and the integrity of remote care systems. 
â€¢ 
Third, CHI supports reasonable software transparency measures, including software bills of 
materials and supply-chain security attestations, as tools for improving resiliency. CHI 
cautions, however, that such requirements be scaled appropriately so that they strengthen 
security without functioning as de facto barriers to entry. Security requirements throughout 
should be risk-proportionate and outcome-focused. 
â€¢ 
Finally, CHI notes that the migration away from one-oP point-to-point connections toward 
standardized, certiï¬ed FHIR APIs is itself a means of improving resiliency. CHI encourages 
CMS to coordinate across ASTP/ONC, the OPice for Civil Rights, and CISA so that payers 
and developers face a single coherent set of expectations rather than overlapping and 
inconsistent mandates. 
 
h. RFI on Improving Implementation of Payer Application Programming Interface 
Technology 
 
CHI supports exploring how the ONC Health IT Certiï¬cation Program, and comparable testing and 
conformance mechanisms, could help payer APIs meet the technical requirements CMS 
establishes. Conformance testing for payer APIs could be modeled on the approach used for 
certiï¬ed health IT, applied in a manner appropriate to payers and developed collaboratively with 
them. CHI supports CMSâ€™ proposal to use automated testing tools to verify conformance7 and 
encourages CMS to make those tools, along with reference implementations and openly accessible 
sandboxes, available to developers without the resources to build private test environments. 
 
 
7 See 91 Fed. Reg. at 19890 (proposed rule section II.A.4.c) (proposing the use of testing tools to ensure conformance 
with the required implementation guides); see also id. at 19896-97 (request for information on improving payer API 
implementation through testing and certiï¬cation, including potential use of the ONC Health IT Certiï¬cation Program). 
6 
 
CHI encourages CMS to work with payers and developers to develop reasonable, achievable 
expectations for API response-time and availability, so that payer APIs perform dependably in 
practice, and to consider appropriate and proportionate transparency around API performance. 
Transparency of this kind, developed collaboratively with industry, can inform CMS oversight and 
give the market useful information while respecting the operational realities that payers face.  
 
CHI also encourages CMS to help ensure that the APIs this rule supports are genuinely usable in 
practice, so that nominal availability translates into real-world functionality for the providers, 
patients, and developers they are meant to serve. To that end, CHI encourages CMS to work with all 
stakeholders, including payers, to identify and address any practical barriers to access, including 
fee or contracting terms that could unintentionally limit usability, in a balanced manner that 
recognizes payersâ€™ legitimate operational and business interests.  
 
i. RFI on Step Therapy 
 
CHI supports using standardized technology and data sharing to help step therapy work more 
smoothly for patients, providers, and payers alike. When a patient changes payers, the voluntary 
transfer of relevant step therapy history through the Payer-to-Payer API can help avoid unnecessary 
repetition of therapies a patient has already completed, which beneï¬ts patients and payers alike by 
reducing duplicative review. CHI encourages CMS to work with payers and developers to 
standardize the data elements needed to evaluate, apply, and honor step therapy criteria, so that 
this information can move through the FHIR-based APIs alongside other prior authorization data 
and so that developers can build to a single speciï¬cation. 
 
j. RFI on Laboratory Tests and Durable Medical Equipment, Prosthetics, 
Orthotics, and Supplies 
 
CHI sees value in eventually extending a standardized, API-based prior authorization approach to 
laboratory tests and to durable medical equipment, prosthetics, orthotics, and supplies (DMEPOS). 
Where coordination among providers, laboratories, and suppliers can be improved and approval 
times shortened, standardized FHIR-based prior authorization and the Provider Access and Payer-
to-Payer APIs may help address those challenges. 
 
CHI encourages CMS to consider, over an appropriate timeframe and in consultation with aPected 
payers and suppliers, bringing laboratory and DMEPOS prior authorization within the same 
framework being established for drugs and non-drug items and services, so that developers can 
build once and so that the necessary documentation can be exchanged through standardized 
interfaces. CHI further encourages CMS to explore transparency and selective-exemption 
approaches that could reduce burden without compromising program integrity, recognizing that the 
design of any such approach, including any relief from repetitive requirements for consistently 
compliant providers, should be developed collaboratively with payers. 
 
 
 
7 
 
IV. 
Conclusion 
 
CHI urges CMS to move forward consistent with the above recommendations. CHI looks forward to 
continued engagement as the rule is ï¬nalized and stands ready to provide additional information or 
to participate in any stakeholder engagement opportunities. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
 
 
 
Brian Scarpelli 
Executive Director 
 
Chapin Gregor 
Policy Counsel 
 
Connected Health Initiative 
1401 K St NW, Suite 501 
Washington, DC 20005

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Connected Health Initiative (CHI); signed by Brian Scarpelli, Executive Director, and Chapin Gregor, Policy Counsel
- **Stakeholder type:** Technology Vendor / Multi-stakeholder coalition
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Broad multi-stakeholder effort including patients, providers, payers, technology innovators, and many small and medium-sized software developers; focused on connected health, interoperability, patient access, digital health, and AI tools.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

CHI broadly supports CMS's standards-based interoperability direction, including electronic PA for drugs, required FHIR implementation guides, NCPDP pharmacy standards, adoption of FHIR for HIPAA PA transactions, centralized endpoint reporting, and extending requirements to FF-SHOP issuers. It asks CMS to coordinate closely with ASTP/ONC, provide realistic phased timelines, keep requirements technology-neutral and lightweight, support testing and conformance tools, and avoid disproportionate burdens on developers, payers, under-resourced providers, and small issuers.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; GENERAL (event notifications, resiliency, payer API implementation, step therapy, lab/DMEPOS)
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** CMS-0062-P; RIN 0938-AV44; 91 Fed. Reg. 19890, 19892, 19893, 19895, 19896, 19896-97; HIPAA Administrative Simplification authority. No CFR sections cited directly.
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR; HL7 FHIR Da Vinci implementation guides; NCPDP SCRIPT, Formulary & Benefit, and Real-Time Prescription Benefit; Patient Access, Provider Directory, Provider Access, Payer-to-Payer, and Prior Authorization APIs; ADT event notifications; ONC Health IT Certification Program; NIST Cybersecurity Framework; HHS Healthcare and Public Health Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals; Health Industry Cybersecurity Practices under Section 405(d); CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities guidance; software bills of materials.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Electronic prior authorization for drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** CHI describes prior authorization as a major source of care delay and administrative cost and supports standardized API-based PA for all drugs, using FHIR for medical-benefit drugs and NCPDP standards for pharmacy-benefit drugs.
- **Specific request:** Finalize electronic PA requirements for all drugs and keep requirements consistent across CMS programs and ASTP/ONC certification criteria.

**Topic 2: Required FHIR implementation guides and version management**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support / Clarify
- **Rationale:** CHI says making HL7 FHIR Da Vinci IGs required reduces variability and gives developers predictable requirements. It supports allowing any unexpired adopted version but warns that overlapping versions require clear schedules.
- **Specific request:** Require the IGs, permit unexpired versions, and coordinate version adoption and expiration timelines with adequate transition overlap.

**Topic 3: FHIR as a HIPAA prior authorization transaction standard**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** CHI supports adopting FHIR and associated guides for referral certification, authorization, and eligibility transactions related to prior authorization. It frames the change as consistent with API-based interoperability and administrative burden reduction.
- **Specific request:** Adopt FHIR for HIPAA PA transactions while coordinating implementation, testing, and transition expectations.

**Topic 4: Centralized payer API endpoint directory**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** CHI argues that APIs cannot deliver full value if developers, providers, and payers must locate endpoints individually. A centralized directory would reduce discovery burden, especially for Payer-to-Payer exchange.
- **Specific request:** Publish an open, standardized, machine-readable, regularly updated endpoint directory and keep payer reporting requirements lightweight.

**Topic 5: Comparable payer-side and provider-side technology standards**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** CHI says interoperability depends on both payer-side and provider-side technology advancing together, supported by conformance testing, performance expectations, and certification alignment.
- **Specific request:** Pair API expectations with appropriate conformance testing, collaborate with payers and developers on achievable performance benchmarks, and phase benchmarks in over adequate timelines.

**Topic 6: FF-SHOP issuer inclusion**
- **Provision ID:** FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** CHI supports comparable protections for small group market QHP enrollees but recognizes meaningful implementation cost and operational complexity for some issuers.
- **Specific request:** Extend requirements to FF-SHOP issuers using a phased, adequately resourced timeline, retain a narrowly tailored exception mechanism, and consider flexibility for genuine new entrants and issuers without prior API implementation.

**Topic 7: Event notifications for value-based care**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** CHI views ADT-style event notifications as high-value for care coordination and readmission reduction, but urges FHIR-based standardization, privacy safeguards, and careful burden calibration.
- **Specific request:** Advance FHIR-forward event notification criteria, align them with standards adopted elsewhere, provide accessible testing tools, and favor collaborative or voluntary approaches over new enforcement obligations.

**Topic 8: Health care resiliency and cybersecurity**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** CHI supports resiliency improvements but cautions against duplicative cybersecurity mandates, especially for rural or under-resourced facilities and small developers.
- **Specific request:** Anchor expectations to existing frameworks, expand cybersecurity safe harbors for donated security tools and training, scale software transparency measures appropriately, and coordinate across ASTP/ONC, OCR, and CISA.

**Topic 9: Payer API implementation, testing, and real-world usability**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** CHI supports automated testing, conformance mechanisms, reference implementations, sandboxes, and reasonable API response-time and availability expectations. It also flags fees and contracting terms as potential barriers to usability.
- **Specific request:** Make automated testing tools, reference implementations, and sandboxes openly available; develop performance expectations collaboratively; and address practical API access barriers in a balanced way.

**Topic 10: Step therapy data sharing**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Support / Clarify
- **Rationale:** CHI says transferring step therapy history through the Payer-to-Payer API can prevent patients from repeating therapies they have already completed after changing payers.
- **Specific request:** Standardize data elements needed to evaluate, apply, and honor step therapy criteria through FHIR-based APIs.

**Topic 11: Lab and DMEPOS prior authorization**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** CHI sees value in extending API-based PA to laboratory tests and DMEPOS if done over an appropriate timeframe and in consultation with affected stakeholders.
- **Specific request:** Consider bringing lab and DMEPOS PA into the same standardized framework, explore transparency and selective exemptions, and develop relief for consistently compliant providers collaboratively with payers.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

**Solicitation Responses:**
- **S1:** CHI supports requiring, rather than recommending, FHIR IGs because mandatory IGs reduce variability and support predictable development.
- **S2:** CHI supports use of unexpired adopted versions but asks CMS and ASTP/ONC to coordinate version adoption and expiration.
- **S3:** CHI asks for clearly communicated transition schedules and adequate overlap where multiple unexpired versions exist.
- **S12:** CHI supports incorporating medical-benefit drugs into the FHIR Prior Authorization API.
- **S14:** CHI supports NCPDP SCRIPT, Formulary & Benefit, and RTPB standards for pharmacy-benefit drugs across impacted payers.
- **S21:** CHI supports extending drug ePA but asks CMS to use realistic implementation timelines and align requirements across programs.
- **S23:** CHI supports endpoint reporting and, while not raising endpoint-specific security objections, separately emphasizes privacy safeguards and cybersecurity alignment.
- **S24:** CHI supports reporting Patient Access, Provider Directory, Provider Access, Payer-to-Payer, and Prior Authorization API endpoints and related information.
- **S26:** CHI asks that endpoint publication be open, standardized, machine-readable, and lightweight for reporting entities.
- **S27:** CHI asks that the endpoint directory be regularly updated.
- **S33:** CHI supports centralized CMS publication of endpoint information as a reliable directory.
- **S37:** CHI identifies implementation challenges around timeline realism, cost, technical complexity, version transitions, testing, and performance expectations.
- **S40:** CHI supports including small group market QHP issuers on FF-SHOPs so patients receive comparable protections across markets.
- **S41:** CHI requests a phased, adequately resourced timeline for FF-SHOP implementation.
- **S42:** CHI supports retaining a narrowly tailored exception mechanism and additional flexibility for new entrants or issuers without prior API implementation.
- **S44:** CHI supports FHIR as appropriate for prior authorization transactions under HIPAA Administrative Simplification.
- **S45:** CHI supports applying FHIR and associated guides to referral certification, authorization, and eligibility transactions related to dental, professional, and institutional PA.
- **S47:** CHI urges workable transition periods and adequate overlap between versions.
- **S49:** CHI highlights small and medium-sized software developers and small issuers as stakeholders that may face disproportionate burden if requirements are not phased and supported.
- **S50:** CHI supports required FHIR Da Vinci IGs and asks for careful version management.
- **S53:** CHI supports phased implementation for performance expectations and complex new requirements.
- **S54:** CHI supports conformance testing, automated testing tools, reference implementations, and sandboxes.
- **S55:** CHI favors collaborative and proportionate approaches, particularly for event notifications and performance expectations, rather than disproportionate enforcement burdens.
- **S60:** CHI supports coordinated standards versioning and expiration across CMS and ASTP/ONC.
- **S61:** CHI calls for coordination across CMS, ASTP/ONC, OCR, and CISA to avoid overlapping or inconsistent mandates.
- **S62:** CHI supports accessible testing tools and certification/conformance mechanisms.
- **S63:** CHI asks for clear expiration schedules and adequate overlap for standards transitions.
- **S66-S82:** CHI responds to several general RFIs, including event notifications, resiliency, payer API implementation, step therapy, and lab/DMEPOS. Across these, it favors FHIR-based standardization, practical testing infrastructure, privacy and cybersecurity safeguards, voluntary/collaborative implementation where appropriate, and burden-sensitive phasing.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize electronic PA requirements for all drugs using FHIR for medical-benefit drugs and NCPDP standards for pharmacy-benefit drugs.
2. Align CMS requirements with ASTP/ONC certification criteria so developers can build once and deploy across settings.
3. Make FHIR Da Vinci IGs required and manage version transitions with clear schedules and adequate overlap.
4. Adopt FHIR and associated guides for HIPAA PA-related referral certification, authorization, and eligibility transactions.
5. Create an open, standardized, machine-readable, regularly updated CMS endpoint directory.
6. Keep endpoint reporting lightweight.
7. Pair API expectations with conformance testing and collaboratively developed performance expectations.
8. Phase in performance benchmarks and complex requirements over adequate timelines.
9. Extend interoperability and PA protections to FF-SHOP issuers with appropriate exceptions and flexibility.
10. Advance FHIR-based event notifications while preserving privacy safeguards and limiting disproportionate enforcement burden.
11. Anchor resiliency expectations to existing cybersecurity frameworks and expand cybersecurity safe harbors.
12. Provide automated testing tools, reference implementations, and open sandboxes for developers.
13. Standardize step therapy data elements for exchange through FHIR APIs.
14. Consider extending standardized API-based PA to laboratory tests and DMEPOS after consultation and over an appropriate timeframe.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Regulatory misalignment, version-transition uncertainty, duplicative implementations, endpoint discovery burden, API usability barriers, disproportionate costs for small developers and issuers, cybersecurity mandate fragmentation, and insufficient testing infrastructure.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Higher development and compliance costs, delayed implementation, barriers to entry, inconsistent API performance, underused APIs despite nominal availability, and avoidable burden on under-resourced providers and facilities.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Multiple versions of standards, endpoint discovery, conformance testing gaps, response-time and availability expectations, fees or contracting barriers, cybersecurity supply-chain transparency burdens, and FF-SHOP issuer readiness.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE
